children: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) kept its 2026 global economic growth outlook unchanged and nudged higher its 2027 forecast while its economists warned the world's economic resilience remains strained.
The picture emerging was that of a global economy hurt by two costly wars and high energy prices while being helped by the hundreds of billions spent on the artificial intelligence buildout.

As policymakers gather in Bangkok for the annual IMF/World Bank meetings, the IMF said it expects global economic growth of 3.1% this year, unchanged from its April forecast, and slightly raised its 2027 target to 3.4%, up from its 3.2% projection in the spring. The IMF still expects inflation this year of 4.7% and 4.1% next year, reinforcing investors' expectations that inflation will stay elevated for the near-term.

IMF economists attributed the still solid global economic growth partly to rerouting of energy supplies as the Iran war continues, as well as economies drawing on energy inventories and economies that have become more energy-efficient. The other reason growth forecasts have held up is because of the AI investment boom in the U.S. and around the world.

But the economists warn that if policymakers don't bolster their supply capacity and replenish their buffers, the global economy is at risk of testing the limits of its resilience. Among the concerns: Countries have drawn down their energy inventories, making them vulnerable to additional geopolitical shocks as the wars in Iran and Ukraine continues. And it isn't just expensive energy that could upend economies around the world but also disruptions from higher fertilizer costs, export restrictions and extreme weather.

On top of that, the IMF economists caution that the same technology-related investment that has boosted growth could become a risk due to growing concentration as a small number of corporate giants, sectors and economies rack up most of the gains. "Global expansion is heavily reliant on a narrow set of technological and financial conditions," warns IMF Economic Counselor Silvana Tenreyro. "More generally, resilience has been uneven, varying noticeably with economies' exposure to the war and the AI boom, and causing divergent outcomes."

Climbing interest rates — fueled by mounting government budget deficits and heavy corporate borrowing for AI spending — are another worry. "The interaction of higher financing costs with elevated debt levels exposes a key margin of vulnerability," the IMF cautions, calling on policymakers to rebuild their buffers. If a major economy loses fiscal credibility or if commodity prices increase, the IMF cautions that global growth would be materially lower than its baseline.

The IMF also highlights the need for countries to build supply-chain resilience amid weather and heightened geopolitical disruptions. It said policymakers should increase investment in critical technologies, diversify trade relationships and create stronger supply buffers for water, energy, food and other essentials.

In an increasingly fragmented world where governments are looking to become self-reliant, the IMF also encouraged the world to continue to cooperate. "In a more shock-prone and still interconnected world, resilience cannot be built by countries acting alone," Tenreyro writes in the outlook.
